---
title: "Lecture 1: Getting Started with GitHub"
---

This lecture will guide you through setting up GitHub and Git for version control. These tools are essential for modern software development and scientific computing.

# Why Version Control?

Version control systems track changes to your files over time. This allows you to:

- **Revert** to previous versions if something goes wrong
- **Collaborate** with others without overwriting each other's work
- **Track** who made what changes and when
- **Backup** your work to the cloud automatically

Git is the most popular version control system, and GitHub is a cloud platform for hosting Git repositories.

---

# Section 1: Create a GitHub Account

## Step 1: Sign Up

1. Go to [github.com](https://github.com)
2. Click **Sign up**
3. Enter your email address (use your **PSU email** for educational benefits)
4. Create a password
5. Choose a username (this will be visible publicly)
6. Complete the verification puzzle
7. Click **Create account**

::: {.callout-tip}
## Educational Benefits
Using your `.edu` email gives you access to [GitHub Education](https://education.github.com/), which includes free GitHub Pro features, free access to various developer tools, and GitHub Copilot.
:::

## Step 2: Verify Your Email

1. Check your email inbox for a verification email from GitHub
2. Click the verification link
3. You now have a GitHub account!

## Step 3: Set Up Your Profile

1. Click your profile icon (top right) → **Settings**
2. Add a profile picture
3. Add your name and bio
4. Click **Update profile**

---

# Section 2: Configure Git

Git needs to know who you are so it can label your commits. Open a terminal and run:

## Set Your Name

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
```

## Set Your Email

Use the same email you used for GitHub:

```bash
git config --global user.email "your.email@psu.edu"
```

## Set Default Branch Name

Modern convention uses `main` instead of `master`:

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

## Verify Your Configuration

```bash
git config --list
```

You should see your name and email listed.

---

# Section 3: Set Up SSH Authentication

SSH keys allow you to connect to GitHub without entering your password every time.

## Step 1: Check for Existing SSH Keys

```bash
ls -la ~/.ssh
```

If you see files like `id_rsa.pub` or `id_ed25519.pub`, you already have SSH keys.

## Step 2: Generate a New SSH Key

If you don't have existing keys, generate one:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@psu.edu"
```

When prompted:
- Press **Enter** to accept the default file location
- Enter a passphrase (optional but recommended)

## Step 3: Start the SSH Agent

```bash
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
```

## Step 4: Add Your Key to the SSH Agent

```bash
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

## Step 5: Copy Your Public Key

**On macOS:**
```bash
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

**On Linux:**
```bash
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```
Then manually copy the output.

**On Windows (Git Bash):**
```bash
clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

## Step 6: Add SSH Key to GitHub

1. Go to [github.com](https://github.com) and log in
2. Click your profile icon → **Settings**
3. In the left sidebar, click **SSH and GPG keys**
4. Click **New SSH key**
5. Give it a descriptive title (e.g., "My Laptop")
6. Paste your public key in the "Key" field
7. Click **Add SSH key**

## Step 7: Test Your Connection

```bash
ssh -T git@github.com
```

You should see: "Hi username! You've successfully authenticated..."

---

# Section 4: Create Your First Repository

## Option A: Create on GitHub (Recommended for Beginners)

1. Go to [github.com](https://github.com)
2. Click the **+** icon → **New repository**
3. Enter a repository name (e.g., `my-first-repo`)
4. Add a description (optional)
5. Choose **Public** or **Private**
6. Check **Add a README file**
7. Click **Create repository**

## Clone to Your Computer

```bash
git clone git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/my-first-repo.git
cd my-first-repo
```

## Option B: Create Locally First

```bash
mkdir my-project
cd my-project
git init
```

Then connect to GitHub:

1. Create an empty repository on GitHub (don't add README)
2. Run:

```bash
git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/my-project.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

---

# Section 5: Basic Git Workflow

The basic Git workflow follows this pattern:

```
Edit files → Stage changes → Commit → Push
```

## Check Status

See what files have changed:

```bash
git status
```

## Stage Changes

Add specific files:

```bash
git add filename.txt
```

Add all changes:

```bash
git add .
```

## Commit Changes

Save your staged changes with a message:

```bash
git commit -m "Add initial project files"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Writing Good Commit Messages

- Use present tense: "Add feature" not "Added feature"
- Be specific: "Fix login button color" not "Fix bug"
- Keep it short (50 characters or less for the subject line)
:::

## Push to GitHub

Upload your commits to GitHub:

```bash
git push
```

## Pull from GitHub

Download changes from GitHub:

```bash
git pull
```

---

# Section 6: Working with Branches

Branches let you work on features without affecting the main code.

## Create a New Branch

```bash
git checkout -b feature-name
```

## Switch Between Branches

```bash
git checkout main
git checkout feature-name
```

## List All Branches

```bash
git branch
```

## Merge a Branch

First, switch to the branch you want to merge into:

```bash
git checkout main
git merge feature-name
```

## Delete a Branch

After merging:

```bash
git branch -d feature-name
```

---

# Summary

You've learned:

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `git config` | Set up your identity |
| `git clone` | Copy a repository |
| `git init` | Create a new repository |
| `git status` | Check what's changed |
| `git add` | Stage changes |
| `git commit` | Save changes |
| `git push` | Upload to GitHub |
| `git pull` | Download from GitHub |
| `git branch` | Work with branches |

## Key Points

- GitHub is a cloud platform for Git repositories
- SSH keys provide secure, password-free authentication
- The basic workflow is: edit → stage → commit → push
- Branches let you work on features independently
- Good commit messages help you and others understand changes

- Complete the [GitHub Hello World](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/quickstart/hello-world) tutorial

- Learn about [Pull Requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests) for collaboration
